title: No. 39 — The Conformity of the Plan to Republican Principles (Madison)
paragraphs: With the last paper we finished the observations meant as an introduction to a fair survey of the plan of government reported by the Convention. We now turn to carrying out that part of our undertaking.

The first question to ask is whether the general form and aspect of the government is strictly republican. Clearly no other form could be reconciled with the spirit of the people of America, with the fundamental principles of the Revolution, or with the honorable resolve, shared by every devotee of liberty, to rest all our political experiments on mankind's capacity for self-government. If the plan of the Convention turns out to depart from the republican character, then, its advocates must give it up as no longer defensible.

What, then, distinguishes the republican form? Suppose we looked for the answer not in principles but in the way political writers have applied the term to the constitutions of different States. We would never find a satisfactory one. Holland, where not a particle of the supreme authority comes from the people, has almost universally been called a republic. The same title has been given to Venice, where a small body of hereditary nobles holds absolute power, and exercises it absolutely, over the great body of the people. Poland, a mixture of aristocracy and monarchy in their worst forms, has been dignified with the same name. England has only one republican branch of government, combined with a hereditary aristocracy and a monarchy, yet it has with equal impropriety often been put on the list of republics. These examples are nearly as unlike one another as they are unlike a genuine republic, and they show how extremely loosely the term has been used in political discussions.

Suppose instead we take as our standard the different principles on which different forms of government are founded. We may then define a republic as, or at least give that name to, a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior. It is ESSENTIAL to such a government that it be derived from the great body of the society, and not from an inconsiderable proportion of it or a favored class. If it were otherwise, a handful of tyrannical nobles who exercised their oppressions by delegating their powers could aspire to the rank of republicans and claim the honorable title of republic for their government. It is SUFFICIENT for such a government that those who administer it be appointed by the people, directly or indirectly, and that they hold their appointments by one of the tenures just named. If that were not enough, every government in the United States would lose its republican character, and so would every other popular government that has been or can be well organized or well executed. In every State in the Union, the constitution provides that some officers of government, at least, are appointed only indirectly by the people. In most of them the chief executive himself is appointed in this way. In one, this mode of appointment reaches even one of the co-ordinate branches of the legislature. In all the constitutions, too, the highest offices are held for a fixed period, and in many cases, in both the legislative and executive departments, for a period of years. Most of the constitutions also provide, as the most respected and accepted opinions on the subject recommend, that the members of the judiciary department keep their offices by the firm tenure of good behavior.

Compare the Constitution planned by the Convention with this standard, and we see at once that it meets it in the strictest sense. The House of Representatives is elected directly by the great body of the people, as at least one branch of every State legislature is. The Senate, like the present Congress and the Senate of Maryland, gets its appointment indirectly from the people. The President is derived indirectly from the choice of the people, following the example of most of the States. Even the judges and all the other officers of the Union will be chosen by the people themselves, though by a remote choice, just as in the individual States. The length of the appointments also accords with the republican standard and with the model of the State constitutions. The House of Representatives is elected at fixed intervals, as in all the States, and for two years, as in the State of South Carolina. The Senate is elected for six years, only one year more than the term of the Senate of Maryland and only two more than that of the Senates of New York and Virginia. The President is to stay in office for four years. In New York and Delaware, by comparison, the chief executive is elected for three years, and in South Carolina for two. In the other States the election is annual. In several of the States, moreover, the constitution makes no provision for impeaching the chief executive, and in Delaware and Virginia he cannot be impeached until he is out of office. The President of the United States can be impeached at any time while in office. The judges are to hold their places, as unquestionably they ought, by the tenure of good behavior. The tenure of ministerial offices in general will be settled by law, as the reason of the case and the example of the State constitutions require.

Should any further proof of the republican complexion of this system be wanted, the most decisive is its absolute prohibition of titles of nobility under both the federal and the State governments, together with its express guaranty of the republican form to each of the State governments.

"But it was not sufficient," say the adversaries of the proposed Constitution, "for the convention to adhere to the republican form. They ought, with equal care, to have preserved the FEDERAL form, which regards the Union as a CONFEDERACY of sovereign states; instead of which, they have framed a NATIONAL government, which regards the Union as a CONSOLIDATION of the States." And it is asked by what authority this bold and radical innovation was undertaken. The use that has been made of this objection means we must examine it with some precision.

I will not stop to ask whether the distinction behind the objection is accurate. To judge the force of the objection fairly, we need to do three things. First, we must find out the real character of the government in question. Second, we must ask how far the Convention was authorized to propose such a government. Third, we must ask how far the duty it owed its country could make up for any lack of regular authority.

First. To find out the real character of the government, we can look at it under five relations: to the foundation on which it is to be established, to the sources from which its ordinary powers are drawn, to the operation of those powers, to their extent, and to the authority by which future changes in the government are to be introduced.

Look at the first relation. On the one hand, the Constitution is to be founded on the assent and ratification of the people of America, given by deputies elected for the special purpose. On the other hand, the people are to give this assent and ratification not as individuals who make up one entire nation, but as the people of the distinct and independent States to which they respectively belong. It is to be the assent and ratification of the individual States, derived from the supreme authority in each State, that is, the authority of the people themselves. So the act establishing the Constitution will not be a NATIONAL act but a FEDERAL one.

One consideration alone shows plainly that it will be a federal and not a national act, as the objectors understand these terms. It will be the act of the people as forming so many independent States, not as forming one aggregate nation, because it is to come neither from the decision of a MAJORITY of the people of the Union nor from that of a MAJORITY of the States. It must come from the UNANIMOUS assent of the individual States that are parties to it. It differs from their ordinary assent only in being expressed by the people themselves rather than by the legislative authority. Suppose the people were regarded in this transaction as forming one nation. Then the will of the majority of all the people of the United States would bind the minority, just as the majority in each State must bind the minority there. That majority would be determined either by comparing the individual votes or by taking the will of the majority of the States as evidence of the will of a majority of the people of the United States. Neither rule has been adopted. Each State, in ratifying the Constitution, is treated as a sovereign body, independent of all the others, and bound only by its own voluntary act. In this relation, then, the new Constitution, if it is established, will be a FEDERAL and not a NATIONAL constitution.

The next relation concerns the sources from which the ordinary powers of government are to be derived. The House of Representatives will draw its powers from the people of America, and the people will be represented in the same proportion and on the same principle as in the legislature of a particular State. So far the government is NATIONAL, not FEDERAL. The Senate, on the other hand, will draw its powers from the States as political and coequal societies, and these will be represented in the Senate on the principle of equality, as they now are in the existing Congress. So far the government is FEDERAL, not NATIONAL. The executive power will come from a very compound source. The States, in their political characters, will make the immediate election of the President. The votes allotted to them follow a compound ratio, which treats them partly as distinct and coequal societies and partly as unequal members of one society. The eventual election, in turn, is to be made by that branch of the legislature composed of the national representatives; yet for this one act they are to be arranged in delegations, one for each of so many distinct and coequal bodies politic. Seen from this side, the government has a mixed character, with at least as many FEDERAL as NATIONAL features.

As it concerns the OPERATION OF THE GOVERNMENT, the difference between a federal and a national government is supposed to be this. In a federal government the powers act on the political bodies that make up the Confederacy, in their political capacities. In a national government they act on the individual citizens who make up the nation, in their individual capacities. Tested by this criterion, the Constitution falls under the NATIONAL character, not the FEDERAL, though perhaps not so completely as has been understood. In several cases, and especially in trying controversies to which States may be parties, the States must be regarded and proceeded against only in their collective and political capacities. To that extent the national countenance of the government on this side seems to be disfigured by a few federal features. But this blemish is perhaps unavoidable in any plan. And because the government acts on the people in their individual capacities in its ordinary and most essential proceedings, we may on the whole call it, in this relation, a NATIONAL government.

Yet if the government is national in the OPERATION of its powers, it changes its aspect once more when we look at the EXTENT of its powers. A national government implies not only authority over the individual citizens but an unlimited supremacy over all persons and things, so far as they can be objects of lawful government. Among a people consolidated into one nation, the national legislature holds this supremacy completely. Among communities united only for particular purposes, it is divided between the general legislature and the municipal legislatures. In the first case, all local authorities are subordinate to the supreme one, which may control, direct or abolish them at pleasure. In the second, the local or municipal authorities hold distinct and independent portions of the supremacy. Within their own spheres they are no more subject to the general authority than the general authority is subject to them within its sphere. In this relation, then, the proposed government cannot be called a NATIONAL one. Its jurisdiction reaches only certain enumerated objects, and it leaves the individual States a residuary and inviolable sovereignty over all the rest. It is true that, when a controversy arises over the boundary between the two jurisdictions, the court with the final decision is to be set up under the general government. But that does not alter the principle. The decision is to be made impartially, by the rules of the Constitution, and all the usual and most effective precautions are taken to secure that impartiality. Some such court is clearly essential to prevent an appeal to the sword and a dissolution of the compact. That it ought to be established under the general government rather than the local governments, or to put it more properly that it could be safely established only under the first, is a position that is unlikely to be disputed.

Test the Constitution by its last relation, to the authority by which amendments are made, and we find it neither wholly NATIONAL nor wholly FEDERAL. If it were wholly national, the supreme and ultimate authority would lie with the MAJORITY of the people of the Union, and that authority could at any time alter or abolish the established government, as the majority of any national society can. If it were wholly federal, every State in the Union would have to concur in any alteration that was to bind them all. The mode the plan of the Convention provides is founded on neither principle. By requiring more than a majority, and particularly by counting the proportion by STATES and not by CITIZENS, it moves away from the NATIONAL character toward the FEDERAL. By making the agreement of fewer than all the States enough, it gives up the FEDERAL character again and takes on the NATIONAL.

The proposed Constitution, therefore, is strictly speaking neither a national nor a federal Constitution but a composition of the two. In its foundation it is federal, not national. In the sources from which the ordinary powers of the government are drawn, it is partly federal and partly national. In the way those powers operate, it is national, not federal. In their extent, once more, it is federal, not national. And finally, in the authoritative mode of introducing amendments, it is neither wholly federal nor wholly national.
